UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
Exelon Corporation 
 
Complainant, 
 
                        v.  
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.  
Respondent. 
 
) 
) 
) 
) 
) 
) 
) 
 
 
 
Docket No. EL27-11-000 
 
 
PRELIMINARY ANSWER OF PJM INTERCONNECTION L.L.C. OPPOSING 
FAST-TRACK PROCESSING AND  
MOTION FOR EXTENSION OF TIME TO ANSWER 
 
Pursuant to Rules 213, 212 and 2008 of the Federal Energy Regulatory 
Commission’s (“Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 PJM Interconnection, 
L.L.C. (“PJM”) respectfully submits this Preliminary Answer to the Complaint Requesting 
Fast-Track Processing (“Complaint”) filed by Exelon Corporation (“Exelon”) on 
November 3, 2026,2 and moves for an extension of time, through December 21, 2026, to 
submit its answer to the Complaint.  This Preliminary Answer only contests the 
Complaint’s request for fast-track processing.  PJM also requests a four-week extension of 
time to answer the Complaint on the merits.  As discussed further below, the Complaint 
raises complex issues that warrant careful consideration, and PJM is currently devoting 
significant resources to ongoing efforts within the PJM Region to develop and file 
substantial revisions to multiple PJM governing documents by the end of the year.3  
 
1 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.213, 385.212 and 385.2008. 
2 Exelon v. PJM, Complaint Requesting Fast Track Processing of Exelon Corporation, Docket No. EL27-11-
000 (Nov. 3, 2026) (“Complaint”).  
3 Capitalized terms used herein and not otherwise defined have the meaning used in the Open Access 
Transmission Tariff, the Amended and Restated Operating Agreement of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., the 
PJM Reliability Assurance Agreement, or the PJM Manuals.

2 
Granting the requested extension will allow PJM to have a meaningful opportunity to fully 
address the issues raised in the Complaint, thereby facilitating a complete and well-
developed record for Commission consideration. 
PJM further requests that the Commission apply the five-day comment period 
applicable to motions for extension of time, such that responses would be due on November 
9, 2026.4  PJM also respectfully requests that the Commission establish the schedule for 
answering the Complaint as promptly as practicable. 
I. 
PRELIMINARY ANSWER OPPOSING FAST-TRACK PROCESSING 
The Complaint requests fast-track processing of its Complaint and asks the 
Commission to find that the existing three-year forward procurement period employed in 
PJM’s Reliability Pricing Model is no longer just and reasonable and to replace it with a 
“prompt” auction construct.  However, the Complaint fails to satisfy the stringent standard 
necessary to justify fast-track processing.  Commission precedent makes clear that fast-
track procedures are generally reserved for comparatively straightforward tariff disputes 
and are not well suited to proceedings involving complex or far-reaching policy issues.5  
To qualify for fast-track processing, a complainant must present “a highly credible claim 
and persuasive showing that standard processes will not be capable of resolving the 
complaint promptly enough to provide meaningful relief.”6  Because expedited schedules 
impose a substantial burden on the parties and can strain the Commission’s resources, fast-
track processing is appropriately reserved for only the most limited circumstances. 
 
4 See 18 C.F.R. § 385.213(d)(1)(i) (“If a motion requests an extension of time or a shortened time period for 
action, then answers to the motion to extend or shorten the time period shall be made within 5 days after the 
motion is filed, unless otherwise ordered.”). 
5 See e.g. Amoco Energy Trading Corp. v. El Paso Natural Gas, 89 FERC ¶ 61,165 (1999). 
6 See Fast Track Procedures, available at https://www.ferc.gov/fast-track-procedures.

3 
The Complaint makes no such showing.  Exelon offers only a single justification 
for its request, asserting that fast-track processing would “facilitate a Commission order by 
no later than January 31, 2027, the day before PJM is scheduled to post planning parameters 
for the 2030/2031 Delivery Year Base Residual Auction.”7  But Exelon never explains why 
a Commission order by that date is necessary to preserve meaningful relief.  Nor could it.  
Even assuming, arguendo, that the Commission were ultimately to conclude that the 
existing three-year forward capacity market construct is unjust and unreasonable, the 
Federal Power Act provides a mechanism to preserve any potential remedy through the 
establishment of a refund effective date, including the January 1, 2027 refund effective 
date requested by Exelon.8  Accordingly, Exelon fails to demonstrate that the 
Commission’s ordinary processes are incapable of providing meaningful relief. 
Fast-track processing is particularly inappropriate here because the Complaint 
challenges a foundational element of PJM’s Reliability Pricing Model.  The issues raised 
by Exelon extend far beyond a discrete tariff interpretation dispute and instead implicate 
fundamental questions regarding several key components of the design and operation of 
PJM’s capacity market.  Evaluation of changes to such rules requires careful consideration 
and input from PJM’s diverse stakeholder body so as to not further exacerbate the resource 
adequacy issues facing the PJM Region.9   
 
7 Complaint at 5. 
8 See Section 206(b) of the Federal Power Act, 16 U.S.C. 824e(b) (“At the conclusion of any proceeding 
under this section, the Commission may order refunds of any amounts paid, for the period subsequent to the 
refund effective date through a date fifteen months after such refund effective date, in excess of those which 
would have been paid under the just and reasonable rate, charge, classification, rule, regulation, practice, or 
contract which the Commission orders to be thereafter observed and in force….”). 
9 PJM disagrees with Exelon’s assertion that a prompt auction is just and reasonable on its own without a 
suite of complementary enhancements needed to produce, in Exelon’s words, “a more durable resource 
adequacy construct that can reliably support the efficient entry and exit of Capacity Resources from the PJM 
Region . . . .”  Complaint at 6-7.

4 
PJM is already evaluating a range of comprehensive reforms to address issues 
related to the Reliability Pricing Model.  As part of that effort, PJM recently released its 
Powering Reliability Through Market Design white paper, which identifies three broad 
pathways for maintaining long-term resource adequacy and reliability in the PJM region.10  
Since issuing the paper, PJM has received extensive feedback from stakeholders and other 
interested parties and is actively evaluating those comments with the objective of 
developing a clear roadmap for market reforms and related Commission filings after a 
stakeholder-informed process. 
In short, this proceeding presents precisely the type of complex and consequential 
issues for which the Commission has historically declined to employ fast-track 
procedures.11  Granting Exelon’s request would unnecessarily hinder the ability of PJM 
and other interested stakeholders to develop and present the factual, technical, and policy 
considerations focused on holistic solutions which should be relevant to the Commission’s 
decision.  The Commission should therefore deny Exelon’s request for fast-track 
processing. 
II. 
MOTION FOR EXTENSION OF TIME 
Absent Commission action, pursuant to Rule 206(f), answers to the Complaint 
would be due twenty days after the Complaint’s filing date, or November 23, 2026.  PJM 
respectfully requests that the Commission extend that deadline by four weeks, until 
December 21, 2026. 
 
10 PJM, Powering Reliability Through Market Design Paper (May 6, 2026), https://www.pjm.com/-
/media/DotCom/library/reports-notices/special-reports/2026/20260506-powering-reliability-through-
market-design.pdf.  
11 Amoco Energy Trading Corp., 89 FERC ¶ 61,165 (1999).

5 
Good cause exists for the requested extension.  First, additional time will permit 
PJM to incorporate into its response the outcome of imminent deliberations by the PJM 
Board regarding the path forward for the Base Residual Auction for the 2030/2031 
Delivery Year.  The PJM Board is scheduled to consider these very issues at its November 
17, 2026 meeting, and the PJM Board’s determinations are expected to substantially inform 
PJM’s position regarding the issues raised in the Complaint.  Allowing PJM’s answer to 
reflect the results of those deliberations will provide the Commission with a more complete 
and informed record. Further, following the PJM Board’s deliberations, PJM anticipates 
providing a timeline that outlines the stakeholder process through which a comprehensive 
package of capacity market enhancements, along with any associated filing(s), will be 
developed and finalized in PJM’s forthcoming answer. 
Second, as discussed further below, Exelon has failed to demonstrate any 
compelling reason for Commission action by the requested January 31, 2027 date.  
Accordingly, granting a modest four-week extension of the answer deadline will not impair 
the Commission’s ability to act under section 206 of the Federal Power Act should it 
ultimately determine that modifications to PJM’s three-year forward capacity market are 
warranted.  Rather, the requested extension will ensure that PJM has a meaningful 
opportunity to fully address the complex issues presented in the Complaint and will better 
position the Commission to consider those issues based on a complete and well-developed 
record.   
A. Legal Consequences Do Not Attach Merely When Planning Parameters Are 
Posted. 
 
Exelon’s request for fast-track processing rests entirely on its assertion that the 
Commission should issue an order before PJM posts the planning parameters for the

6 
2030/2031 Base Residual Auction on January 31, 2027.  Implicit in that argument is the 
suggestion that Commission action after that date could run afoul of the prohibition against 
retroactive ratemaking.  That suggestion is unfounded. 
Both the Commission and the courts evaluate retroactivity under the rubric 
established by the Supreme Court in Landgraf v. USI Film Products.12  The salient question 
under Landgraf is at what point in the auction process would a change in the capacity 
auction rules attach new legal consequences.13  As the Supreme Court explained, a rule is 
impermissibly retroactive where it “would impair rights a party possessed when he acted, 
increase a party’s liability for past conduct, or impose new duties with respect to 
transactions already completed.”14  Applying those principles in the capacity market 
context, the critical question is not when planning parameters are posted, but when Market 
Participants take action in reliance on those parameters that carries legal consequences.  
Those consequences do not arise merely because PJM posts planning parameters.  Rather, 
they arise when Market Participants submit binding offers into the auction.  Indeed, PJM’s 
Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) already provides express authority to update 
the planning parameters in certain circumstances.15 
 
12 Landgraf v. USI Film Products, 511 U.S. 244 (1994).  See Affirmed Energy, LLC v. FERC, 166 F.4th 1070 
(D.C. Cir. 2026), PJM Power Providers Group v. FERC, 96 F.4th 390, 398-399 (3d. Cir. 2024) (noting that 
courts routinely apply Landgraf's well-worn retroactivity principles to all sorts of agency actions — including 
FERC’s), and Basin Elec. Power Coop., 177 FERC ¶ 63,020 (2021).  
13 PJM Power Providers Group v. FERC, 96 F.4th at 398 (quoting Landgraf, 511 U.S. at 269-70, 280). 
14 Landgraf, 511 U.S. at 280. 
15 See e.g. Tariff, Attachment DD, section 5.11(a) (requiring PJM to post “[t]he PJM Region Reliability 
Requirement, and the Variable Resource Requirement Curve for the PJM Region, including the details of 
any adjustments to account for Price Responsive Demand and any associated PRD Reservation Prices”).

7 
The Third Circuit’s decision in PJM Power Providers Group v. FERC confirms 
this distinction.16  There, the court held that a tariff revision approved by the Commission 
during the conduct of a capacity auction was impermissibly retroactive because PJM had 
already opened the offer window and Market Participants had submitted binding offers 
based on the previously posted planning parameters.17  Under those circumstances, the 
Commission’s action altered the legal consequences of conduct that had already occurred, 
thereby “nullif[ying] a legal consequence attached to a past action taken in the Auction.”18  
Significantly, the court did not hold that legal consequences attach upon the mere posting 
of planning parameters.  To the contrary, the court’s reasoning focused on the fact that 
Market Participants had already taken binding action in reliance on those parameters.  The 
prohibition against retroactive ratemaking therefore protects reliance interests that arise 
once Capacity Market Sellers submit binding offers, not merely expectations that may exist 
before any such action occurs.19   
This distinction reflects the underlying purpose of the filed-rate doctrine and the 
rule against retroactive ratemaking, which is to promote stability and predictability in 
regulated markets.20  While the posting of planning parameters may inform market 
expectations, expectations alone do not create vested rights or legal consequences.  As the 
 
16 PJM Power Providers Group v. FERC, 96 F.4th at 399._ 
17 Id. at 402. 
18 Id. at 401. 
19 See ISO New Eng. Inc., 196 FERC ¶ 61,172, at P 43 (2026) (rejecting claim of retroactive rate making and 
explaining that in the PJM Power Providers decision the court explained that "retroactive rules alter the past 
legal consequences of past actions" and found that that [PJM] tariff change was retroactive “because it altered 
the legal consequence attached to a past action when it allowed PJM to use a different LDA Reliability 
Requirement than the one it had calculated and posted.”).  
20 PJM Power Providers Group v. FERC, 96 F.4th at 402.

8 
D.C. Circuit has explained, the rule against retroactive ratemaking “does not protect a 
utility’s expectation that a rate will not change in the future.”21  
Accordingly, Exelon has failed to demonstrate why Commission action is required 
by January 31, 2027.  The posting of planning parameters, standing alone, does not 
establish the type of completed transaction or legally consequential market conduct that 
would later constrain the Commission’s ability to act.  In short, the Commission need not 
adopt an expedited schedule to preserve its authority under section 206 of the Federal 
Power Act to order changes to PJM’s capacity market if it ultimately determines that such 
changes are warranted. 
B. Market Participants Receive Adequate Prior Notice Upon Establishment of 
the Refund Effective Date So Any Posted Planning Parameters May Be 
Subject to Revision Under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act 
 
Apart from the fact that no legal consequences attach merely upon the posting of 
planning parameters, Exelon brought this proceeding under section 206 of the FPA.  Under 
the statutory framework established by Congress, the FPA expressly contemplates that 
rates, rules, and practices subject to a section 206 complaint remain subject to Commission 
review and potential modification following the establishment of a refund effective date.  
Upon the filing of a complaint and the establishment of a refund effective date, Market 
Participants are placed on notice that the challenged rate, term, or condition may ultimately 
be found unjust and unreasonable and that the Commission may order prospective relief, 
as well as refunds dating back to the refund effective date.22  
 
21 Louisiana Public Service Commission v. FERC, 10 F.4th 839 (D.C. Cir. 2021) (“the rule against retroactive 
rate making does not protect a utility’s expectation that a rate will not change in the future.”). 
22 16 U.S.C. § 824e(b).

9 
The D.C. Circuit recently reaffirmed this principle, explaining that section 206(b) 
operates as a statutory “exception to the filed-rate doctrine’s general prohibition of 
retroactive rate modifications” and authorizes the Commission to provide relief reaching 
back to the refund effective date established upon the filing of a complaint.23  There, the 
court emphasized that the refund effective date serves a critical notice function because it 
informs Market Participants that the challenged tariff provision is subject to potential 
Commission revision and refund liability from that point forward.24  
Thus, even assuming, arguedo, that the legal consequences attach when planning 
parameters are posted, section 206 independently defeats any claim that Commission 
action after that date would constitute impermissible retroactive ratemaking.  The D.C. 
Circuit has expressly rejected the notion that the filed-rate doctrine bars Commission action 
under section 206 of the FPA.25  That is, Congress specifically authorized the Commission, 
through section 206, to modify existing rates and provide refund relief after establishing a 
refund effective date, thereby placing all affected parties on notice that the challenged rate 
structure remains provisional pending resolution of the complaint.  To be clear, the 
Commission has historically been reluctant to order refunds with respect to final market 
results, and PJM has opposed such requests for refund relief.  PJM references the Court’s 
decision solely to demonstrate that the Commission need not issue an order on the 
underlying complaint prior to PJM posting the planning parameters. 
 
23 Maryland Office of People's Counsel v. FERC, 164 F.4th 920, 927 (D.C. Cir. 2026) (internal quotation 
markets removed). 
24 Id. at 928-30. 
25 Id. at 927.

10 
The filing of Exelon’s section 206 complaint put Market Participants on notice that 
PJM’s existing capacity market construct challenged by the Complaint may ultimately be 
modified by Commission order.  Accordingly, once the refund effective date is established, 
stakeholders have legally sufficient notice that the existing rules may be revised and that 
any resulting relief may relate back to that date.  Exelon therefore cannot demonstrate that 
Commission action is required by January 31, 2027, to preserve the Commission’s 
authority to grant meaningful relief.  For that reason as well, Exelon’s request for fast-track 
processing should be denied and the Commission should grant a four-week extension of 
time to answer Exelon’s complaint. 
C. PJM is Scheduled to Post Planning Parameters By March 1, 2027 for the 
2030/2031 Base Residual Auction. 
 
Further undermining Exelon’s claim of urgency, the Commission recently accepted 
Tariff revisions that require PJM to post the PJM Region Reliability Requirement and the 
Locational Deliverability Area Reliability Requirement by March 1 preceding each Base 
Residual Auction.26  Consistent with that order and the updated Tariff,27 PJM will revise 
its pre-auction schedule and now anticipates posting the planning parameters for the 
2030/2031 Base Residual Auction on or before March 1, 2027.  Accordingly, even if the 
Commission were to conclude that action should be taken before the planning parameters 
for the 2030/2031 Base Residual Auction are posted, the Commission would have until 
February 28, 2027, rather than January 31, 2027, to act (i.e., four extra weeks).  Exelon’s 
asserted deadline therefore no longer reflects PJM’s anticipated pre-auction schedule for 
posting the planning parameters. 
 
26 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Delegated Letter Order, Docket No. ER26-3661-000 (Oct. 30, 2026). 
27 See Tariff, Attachment DD, section 5.10(a)(iv)(B).

11 
For this additional reason, granting PJM’s request for a four-week extension of time 
to answer the Complaint, through December 21, 2026, will not prejudice any party, 
constrain the Commission’s consideration of the issues presented, or otherwise impair the 
Commission’s ability to exercise its authority under section 206 of the Federal Power Act 
should it ultimately determine that changes to PJM’s capacity market rules are warranted. 
III. 
CONCLUSION 
For the reasons set forth herein, PJM respectfully requests that the Commission 
deny Exelon’s request for fast-track processing.  PJM further requests that the Commission 
promptly grant PJM’s request for an extension of time, through December 21, 2026, to 
answer the Complaint.  Good cause exists for the requested four-week extension as it will 
afford PJM and other interested parties a meaningful opportunity to review, analyze, and 
respond to the significant legal, policy, and market-design issues raised by the Complaint.  
Granting the requested extension will facilitate the development of a comprehensive and 
well-supported record upon which the Commission can base its determination.

12 
 
Finally, the requested extension will not prejudice any party or impair the 
Commission’s ability to grant relief, if warranted.  As discussed above, the extension has 
no effect on the Commission’s authority under section 206 of the Federal Power Act28 to 
establish a refund effective date and, if appropriate, order relief in this proceeding.  
Accordingly, for good cause shown, the Commission should deny Exelon’s request for 
fast-track processing, grant PJM’s motion for an extension of time, and establish December 
21, 2026, as the deadline for answers to the Complaint. 
 
Respectfully submitted,
